newsitem.title: UK: 50 more years of IRA bombs won't budge us - Major.
newsitem.headline: 50 more years of IRA bombs won't budge us - Major.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major said on Wednesday Britain would not give way to violence even if the Irish Republican Army continued its bombing campaign for another 50 years.

He said he was confident that a deadlock in the Northern Irish peace process could be ended but insisted that Britain would not be swayed by bombs into allowing the IRA's Sinn Fein political wing to join in peace talks.
"If the IRA continues with violence for the next 50 years then Britain would not change its policy in the face of that violence for the next 50 years," Major said.
"The British government's position would be unmovable," he told the Belfast Telegraph newspaper.
"You cannot bomb Britain out of a political position and you cannot bomb your way into the objectives that Sinn Fein seek."

Major, making a traditional Christmas visit to troops and community leaders in the British province, said he was totally committed to the three-year drive to end a decades-old conflict which has claimed more than 3,200 lives.

"We have now hit a hurdle but I think it is a hurdle we will be able to overcome. We have done so in the past. I have every intention of trying to do so again," he told reporters after visiting a school in the town of Dungannon near Belfast.
"I don't believe people can stand in the way of that progress. It may be slow, it may be painful but progress I am confident there will be," he said.
Major's optimism is not shared by many local politicians and security analysts, who are gloomy about the short-term prospects for peace in the war-weary region.
The IRA shows no sign of restoring a ceasefire it abandoned last February and multi-party talks that have limped along since June were adjourned on Wednesday for Christmas until January 13.

In a statement, the joint chairmen of the multi-party talks -- former U.S. senator George Mitchell, General John de Chastelain of Canada and former Finnish prime minister Harri Holkeri -- regretted more headway had not been made.

"We wish it were possible to report more rapid and more meaningful progress. But although the issues are difficult and progress is slow, we remain convinced that this (talks) process offers the best, indeed the only, way forward.

"We also remain convinced that with renewed determination and effort by all of the participants, substantial progress can be made on the issues of (guerrilla arms) decommissioning and also on the ultimate issue of an agreed settlement."
Britain insists the IRA must declare a truce before Sinn Fein is allowed into the talks. Sinn Fein wants talks without preconditions.

Major, on his first visit since Irish Republican Army bombers killed a soldier in a car bomb attack on British army headquarters south of Belfast last October, said: "I hope from where we are that we will be able to move forwards."

The October bombing at the military garrison was the first attack in the province for two years by IRA guerrillas who are fighting to end British rule. It came nine months after they went back to a war footing with bombs on mainland Britain.

Northern Ireland's 60 per cent Protestant majority strongly supports rule from London, but the Catholic minority, some of whom back the IRA and its Sinn Fein political arm, want an all-Ireland state ruled from Dublin.
